summary: In Greek and Roman mythology, Pyramus (Ancient Greek Πύραμος) is one of the ill-fated Babylonian lovers whose story survives fullest in Ovid's Metamorphoses. Forbidden by rival parents to marry Thisbe, he arranged a night tryst at Ninus's tomb; mistaking her blood-stained cloak for proof of her death, he fell on his sword and stained the white mulberry fruits dark red. This atlas node is the youth of the Ovidian lovers' tale, not the Cilician river Pyramos.
attribution: Adapted from Wikipedia, "Pyramus and Thisbe" · CC BY-SA 4.0
etymology: Ancient Greek Púramos (Πύραμος). The same name designates the Ceyhan River in Cilicia; an older aetiological version transformed the lovers into that river and a nearby spring rather than ending in double suicide under a mulberry.

sections.heading: Identity
paragraphs: Ovid places Pyramus and Thisbe in Semiramis's Babylon as the fairest youth and maiden of the eastern city. Rival parents forbade their marriage; the pair whispered vows through a crack in the shared wall between their houses. This atlas entry follows that tragic youth; the historical Greek name Pyramos for the Cilician Ceyhan River preserves an older metamorphosis tradition in which he becomes the river and Thisbe a spring.

sections.heading: Ovid's tale
paragraphs: They planned to meet by night at Ninus's tomb under a mulberry tree. Thisbe arrived first, fled a lioness fresh from a kill, and dropped her cloak. Pyramus found the torn, bloodied garment and the beast's tracks, believed Thisbe dead, and stabbed himself; his blood darkened the white mulberries. When Thisbe returned and found him dying, she prayed that they be buried together and killed herself with the same sword. The gods honored her prayer: the fruit stayed dark, and their ashes shared one urn.

sections.heading: Origins and reception
paragraphs: Ovid's version (Metamorphoses 4.55–166), published in 8 AD, is the oldest surviving full account but adapts an existing aetiology. A second-century mosaic near Nea Paphos and a progymnasma by Nicolaus Sophista preserve the river-and-spring metamorphosis. Hyginus lists Pyramus among those who died for love of Thisbe.

The tale fed medieval and Renaissance romance: Chaucer and Gower retell it in English; Boccaccio adapts the wall-crack motif; Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet inherits the mistaken-death suicides, while A Midsummer Night's Dream burlesques the lovers as a play-within-the-play. Later adaptations include Góngora, Théophile de Viau, Baroque opera, Rostand's Les Romanesques (source of The Fantasticks), and modern retellings in popular culture.
